neighbours.label: the verb 'take' (take/took/taken) heading an idiom completed by a particle or fixed object: take on, take over, take the place of, take place; literal 'take' + duration or object is weak
fire: With the founder retiring, her daughter has taken on the running of the shop.
Frozen peas can take the place of fresh ones in this soup.
A new conductor will take over the orchestra next season.
As the sauce reduces it will take on a deep red colour.
The ceremony will take place on the lawn if the weather holds.
When the mayor fell ill, his deputy took over the daily meetings.
No machine can take the place of a patient teacher.
The younger players have taken on more responsibility this year.
quiet: With the founder retiring, her daughter has accepted the running of the shop.
Frozen peas can replace fresh ones in this soup.
A new conductor will lead the orchestra next season.
As the sauce reduces it will turn a deep red colour.
The drive to the coast will take about four hours in traffic.
When the mayor fell ill, his deputy took a train to the capital.
Please take your shoes off the sofa before you sit down.
It took two men to carry the piano up the stairs.

notes: Four near misses keep the word 'take' in a literal use (duration, object) and four swap the verb. The + pole fires on verbs before the particle 'in' (ring in, usher in, zero in), so the unit seems to track verb+particle idioms, with 'take' on this side. Probes: take on/the place 0.75-0.87, take over 0.54, take place 0.36; took a walk 0.17, take three hours 0.09.
